title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: The prevention of loss to life and property due to natural calamities is being viewed very seriously by the Government of India. In the past, the main role played by the Government in the case of various disasters was confined mainly to post-disaster activities that included providing relief and organising rehabilitation. The Uttarkashi Earthquake of 1991, Killari Earthquake of 1993 and the devastating Malpa landslide along the Kailash-Mansarovar route in 1998 acted as an eye-opener for the Government. The need was felt for a proactive approach rather than waiting for a disaster to occur. The Disaster Management Act, 2005, was enacted on 23 December 2005 and the National Disaster Management Authority, a statutory body under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister, was set up. As per the Disaster Management Act, the responsibility to cope with natural disasters is essentially that of state governments and the role of the central government is a supportive one in terms of supplementing physical and financial resources.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
section_title: Executive Summary — Landslide Risk in India
text: Landslides are one of the natural hazards that affect at least 15 per cent of the land area of India — an area which exceeds 0.49 million sq. km. Landslides of different types are frequent in geodynamically active domains in the Himalayan and Arakan-Yoma belt of the North-Eastern parts of the country as well as in the relatively stable domains of the Meghalaya Plateau, Western Ghats and Nilgiri Hills. In all, 22 states and parts of the Union Territory of Puducherry and Andaman & Nicobar Islands are affected by this hazard. The phenomenon of landslides is pronounced during the monsoon period. In 2005 alone, more than 500 human lives were lost due to this hazard in the country.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
section_title: Nine Major Areas for Landslide Hazard Management
text: The Guidelines identify nine major areas for systematic and coordinated management of landslide hazards: (i) landslide hazard, vulnerability and risk assessment; (ii) multi-hazard conceptualisation; (iii) landslide remediation practice; (iv) research and development, monitoring and early warning; (v) knowledge network and management; (vi) capacity building and training; (vii) public awareness and education; (viii) emergency preparedness and response; and (ix) regulation and enforcement.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Landslide hazard and risk assessment is carried out through landslide hazard zonation (LHZ) mapping and geological and geotechnical investigation of vulnerable slopes and existing landslides. Hazard zonation mapping involves creation of a landslide inventory, selecting scales for mapping depending on end-user requirements, selecting landslide hazard zonation methodologies for different scales, multi-hazard integration (especially integrating seismic hazard), prioritisation of areas for LHZ mapping, and landslide risk zonation. Maps of 1:1,00,000 or 1:50,000 scale are considered indicative only and inappropriate for detailed local decisions; larger scale maps at 1:10,000 or 1:5,000 are used for detailed local-level studies.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Landslide risk treatment is the ultimate objective of the risk management process. It comprises a five-pronged strategy: (i) treating vulnerable slopes and existing hazardous landslides; (ii) restricting development in landslide-prone areas; (iii) preparing codes for excavation, construction and grading; (iv) protecting existing developments; and (v) monitoring and warning systems, together with arrangements for landslide insurance and compensation for losses. Risk treatment of already distressed slopes includes four broad types of remediation practice: control works, restraint works, slope protection works, and mass improvement techniques.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
section_title: Human Settlements in Landslide Prone Areas
text: As the growth of urban, semi-urban and rural centres, infrastructural developments, and other developmental activities in landslide-prone areas increases, the risk of landslides rises manifold unless mitigation issues are addressed adequately. District plans for land use may be developed to minimise the risk of landslide hazard. Rules included in state plans control various aspects of development in landslide hazard-prone areas, including design, construction, location and density, and include provisions to ensure that risk does not increase due to unplanned urbanisation, intensified improper land use, or new construction in high-hazard areas.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Early warning is a process involving three components: (i) scientific and technical communities; (ii) government authorities and civil agencies; and (iii) local communities. Involvement of local communities is crucially important — an aware and vigilant community sensitised to the warning signs of impending landslides is a vital pillar for implementation of an effective early warning system. Real-time monitoring may be undertaken for a few devastating, large-dimension and recurring slides or rock falls that are difficult to stabilise and pose a high risk.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: The Geological Survey of India (GSI) was declared the nodal agency for landslides by the Government in January 2004, with responsibility for coordinating activities related to landslide hazard mitigation and monitoring landslide occurrence in the country. The Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the Ministry of Environment and Forests were identified as nodal agencies for geotechnical investigations and land-use zonation and regulation respectively, following task forces set up after the 1998 Malpa tragedy.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Hazard: a threatening event or the probability of occurrence of a potentially damaging phenomenon within a given time period and area. Vulnerability: the degree of loss to a given element at risk resulting from the occurrence of a natural or man-made phenomenon of a given magnitude, expressed on a scale from 0 (no damage) to 1 (total loss). Risk: the anticipated number of lives in danger, damage to property and disruption of economic activity due to a particular natural phenomenon. Landslide Hazard Zonation Map: map of spatial and temporal extent of landslide hazard indicating areas that are, or could be, affected by landslides, assessing the probability of occurrence within a specific period. Landslide Risk Map: a map that integrates landslide hazard, landslide vulnerability and quantification of elements at risk.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: India is highly vulnerable to floods and out of the total geographical area of 329 million hectares, more than 40 million hectares is flood prone. Floods are a recurrent phenomenon, which cause huge loss of lives and damage to livelihood systems, property, infrastructure and public utilities. The average annual flood damage during 1996-2005 was Rs. 4,745 crore, compared to Rs. 1,805 crore, the corresponding average for the preceding 53 years — an increase attributed to rapid population growth, urbanisation, and growing developmental and economic activity in flood plains, alongside global warming.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Floods have been a recurrent phenomenon in India and cause huge losses to lives, properties, livelihood systems, infrastructure and public utilities. On an average every year, 75 lakh hectares of land is affected, about 1,600 lives are lost, and the damage caused to crops, houses and public utilities is around Rs. 1,805 crore due to floods. The maximum number of lives (11,316) were lost in the year 1977. The frequency of major floods is more than once in five years, and floods have also occurred in areas which were earlier not considered flood-prone.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Flooding in cities and towns is caused by increasing incidence of heavy rainfall in a short period of time, indiscriminate encroachment of waterways, inadequate capacity of drains and lack of maintenance of drainage infrastructure. NDMA has recognised urban flooding as an issue meriting exclusive attention, with separate guidelines for its management prepared and issued.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
section_title: Objectives of the Flood Management Guidelines
text: The Guidelines rest on objectives including: shifting the focus to preparedness through a time-bound, techno-economically viable, socially acceptable and eco-friendly combination of structural and non-structural flood management measures; ensuring regular monitoring of the effectiveness and sustainability of flood-control structures; continuous modernisation of flood forecasting, early warning and decision-support systems; ensuring flood-resistant features in new structures in flood-prone areas; drawing up time-bound flood-proofing plans for strategic and public utility structures; improving awareness and preparedness of stakeholders; introducing capacity-development interventions; improving the compliance regime; and strengthening emergency response capabilities.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
section_title: Institutional Framework — National Disaster Management Authority
text: Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the NDMA, as the apex body, is mandated to lay down policies, plans and guidelines for disaster management to ensure timely and effective response to disasters. Its statutory functions include laying down policies on disaster management, approving the national plan and plans of central ministries and departments, laying down guidelines to be followed by state authorities in drawing up state plans, coordinating enforcement and implementation of policy, recommending funds for mitigation, and exercising general superintendence of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF).

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Unplanned and unregulated developmental activities in flood plains and encroachments into waterways have led to increases in both flood losses and flood risk. Flood plain zoning regulations, based on a model bill circulated by the Central Water Commission (CWC) since 1975, have not been enacted and enforced by most states; only Rajasthan and Manipur have passed such legislation, and even in those cases steps for enforcement have not been taken.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Identified gaps include: non-availability of close contour maps and digital elevation models of flood-prone areas; a flood forecasting and warning network that does not cover all flood-prone rivers and rivulets; most state governments lacking their own reliable forecasting networks; flood plain zoning regulations not enacted by most states; unsatisfactory implementation of flood-proofing measures such as raising villages and constructing flood shelters; reservoir operation often disregarding flood moderation; and lack of inflow forecasting systems for reservoirs, leading to sudden releases that cause downstream flooding.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: The central and state governments are required to take steps for capacity development for effective and sustainable preventive, preparatory and mitigative measures in the pre-flood stage, and for prompt and effective response during and after floods. An effective and prompt response is important for minimising loss of life and property, with communities and NGOs playing a vital role in search, rescue and relief operations, alongside the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) constituted under the DM Act, 2005 for specialised response.

title: National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Floods
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India
text: Since 1954, 33,928 km of new embankments and 38,809 km of drainage channels have been constructed in the country. In addition, 2,450 town protection works have been completed and 4,721 villages have been raised above flood levels. These works have given reasonable protection to an area of about 18.22 million hectares, though the remaining flood-prone area is yet to be protected.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: Section 11 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005 mandates that there shall be a National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP) for the whole of India. The NDMP complies with the National Policy on Disaster Management (NPDM) of 2009 and conforms to the provisions of the DM Act, making it mandatory for central ministries and departments to have adequate disaster management plans. The NDMP is implemented in a scalable manner across all phases of disaster management: mitigation (prevention and risk reduction), preparedness, response, and recovery (immediate restoration to long-term building back better).

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: The NDMP rests on five main pillars: (I) conforming to the national legal mandates — the DM Act 2005 and the National Policy on Disaster Management 2009; (II) participating proactively in global goals under agreements to which India is a signatory — the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change; (III) the Prime Minister's Ten-Point Agenda for Disaster Risk Reduction; (IV) social inclusion as a cross-cutting principle; and (V) mainstreaming disaster risk reduction as an integral feature of development planning.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: The NDMP's vision is to make India disaster resilient across all sectors, achieve substantial and inclusive disaster risk reduction by building local capacities starting with the poor, and decrease significantly the loss of lives, livelihoods, and assets — economic, physical, social, cultural, and environmental — while enhancing the ability to cope with disasters at all levels of administration and among communities.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
section_title: Relocation as Part of Physical Rehabilitation
text: Under the Recovery and Building Back Better chapter, physical rehabilitation activities following a disaster include relocation, social rehabilitation, revival of educational activities, rehabilitation of the elderly, women, children and persons with disabilities, economic rehabilitation, and psychological rehabilitation. The NDMP treats relocation as one component within a broader recovery and rehabilitation process rather than a standalone action.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: The overall coordination of disaster management vests with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), headed by the Prime Minister, is the apex body responsible for laying down policies and guidelines for disaster management and approving the National Disaster Management Plan and the plans of central ministries and departments. The National Executive Committee (NEC) assists the NDMA, prepares the National Plan, and coordinates response in the event of any threatening disaster situation.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
section_title: Institutional Framework — State and District Level
text: Each State/Union Territory has a State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA), headed by the Chief Minister, responsible for laying down state-level policies and plans and approving the State Disaster Management Plan in accordance with NDMA guidelines. At the district level, the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), headed by the District Collector/Magistrate/Deputy Commissioner with the elected representative of the local authority as co-chairperson, acts as the planning, coordinating and implementing body for disaster management in the district.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: The Government of India has notified specific central ministries as nodal agencies for the management and mitigation of different disasters. The Ministry of Jal Shakti is the nodal ministry for floods; the Ministry of Mines is the nodal ministry for landslides; the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs for urban floods; the Ministry of Earth Sciences for cyclones/tornadoes, earthquakes and tsunamis; and the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare for drought, cold wave, frost and hailstorm.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
section_title: Social Inclusion in Disaster Risk Reduction
text: The preamble of the National Policy on Disaster Management 2009 notes that economically weaker and socially marginalised sections, women, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and minorities tend to suffer disproportionately during disasters. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 specifically forbids all forms of discrimination — based on sex, caste, community, descent or religion — in any aspect of disaster management. Social inclusion is treated as equality of rights and opportunities, dignity of the individual, and contributing to resilience for everyone regardless of age, gender, disability or other status.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: According to the National Policy on Disaster Management 2009, the primary responsibility for disaster management, including undertaking rescue, relief and rehabilitation measures during a disaster, lies with the State Governments; the Union Government supplements state efforts through logistic and financial support. Centrally allocated finances are largely limited to the National Disaster Response Fund and State Disaster Response Fund, meant for immediate relief and emergency response after a disaster; disaster risk reduction mainstreaming is expected to be funded through the regular developmental budgets of central ministries and state/UT agencies rather than a separate dedicated allocation.

title: National Disaster Management Plan (Revised Edition)
source: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
text: Measures under the NDMP are grouped into short-term (T1, ending 2022), medium-term (T2, ending 2027) and long-term (T3, ending 2030) time frames, aligned with the end year of the Sendai Framework, the Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement. The designations of short, medium and long term refer to time needed for completion and do not signify an order of priority; many actions run concurrently rather than sequentially.

title: National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
section_title: Objectives of the National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
text: The objectives of the National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007 are: to minimise displacement and to promote, as far as possible, non-displacing or least-displacing alternatives; to ensure adequate rehabilitation packages and expeditious implementation of the rehabilitation process with the active participation of affected families; to ensure that special care is taken for protecting the rights of the weaker sections of society, especially members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and to create obligations on the State for their treatment with concern and sensitivity; to provide a better standard of living by making concerted efforts towards providing sustainable income to affected families; to integrate rehabilitation concerns into the development planning and implementation process; and, where displacement is on account of land acquisition, to facilitate a harmonious relationship between the requiring body and the affected families through mutual cooperation.

title: National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
text: The National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007 (NRRP-2007) was formulated by the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India, and came into force with its publication in the Gazette of India on 31 October 2007. The policy has been circulated to various States and Union Territories for implementation, and its provisions provide for the basic minimum requirements that all projects leading to involuntary displacement must address; State Governments, public sector undertakings and other requiring bodies are free to offer benefit levels greater than those prescribed in the Policy.

title: National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
text: The principles of the Policy apply to the rehabilitation and resettlement of families involuntarily and permanently displaced, whether the displacement arises from land acquisition or from any other reason. The Policy covers all cases of involuntary displacement and introduced a Social Impact Assessment (SIA) requirement for displacement affecting large numbers of families (historically referenced thresholds of the order of 400 families in plain areas and 200 families in tribal, hilly or Scheduled Areas), reflecting an intent that larger-scale, more consequential displacement receive more rigorous upfront assessment.

title: National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
text: The main categories of benefits available to affected families under the Policy include, where possible, land for land as compensation; skill development support and preference in project-related jobs (subject to availability of vacancies and suitability of the affected person), generally interpreted as at least one person per nuclear family; a rehabilitation grant in lieu of land or a job; an option for shares in companies implementing the project; and housing benefits for affected families. For linear acquisitions such as roads or railway lines, an ex-gratia payment in addition to compensation has been applied in practice, rather than the full package designed for large-scale, area-based displacement.

title: National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
text: The Policy provides for the appointment of an Administrator and a Commissioner for Rehabilitation and Resettlement, along with their powers and functions; the preparation of a Rehabilitation and Resettlement Plan for affected areas; the specification of Rehabilitation and Resettlement Benefits for Affected Families; a grievance redressal mechanism for affected persons; and a monitoring mechanism to track implementation of resettlement commitments over time.

title: National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007
source: Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India
text: Although the National Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2007 was primarily framed around displacement caused by land acquisition for development projects, its stated principles — minimising displacement, ensuring adequate and expeditious rehabilitation, protecting the rights of weaker sections including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and integrating rehabilitation concerns into planning — are the reference framework commonly cited when grounding disaster-driven relocation and resettlement planning in existing national policy, since India does not have a separate national resettlement policy specific to disaster-induced relocation.
